The Fan-tailed gerygone (Gerygone flavolateralis) is a small passerine bird endemic to the islands of New Caledonia and Vanuatu, where it inhabits humid forest and secondary growth. Egg volume at the start of development has been measured at 1.363 milliliters , a value consistent with the species' relatively small body size among Australasian warblers. The incubation period under controlled conditions is 18 days [ab = 18 days] when eggs are maintained at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration typical for acanthizids of comparable mass. Freshly laid eggs weigh approximately 1.2 grams [Ww0 = approximately 1.2 grams], reflecting the modest investment per offspring in this multi-brooded lineage. After emerging from the egg, the altricial nestling attains a wet weight at birth averaging 1.137 grams [Wwb = 1.137 grams], a value that underscores the highly altricial state of hatchlings. This initial mass is low even among gerygones, suggesting that maternal provisioning during incubation is tightly constrained by the thermal environment.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the nestling phase proceeds rapidly. Fledging, characterised by first flight achievement and departure from the nest, occurs at 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching], a short developmental interval that is adaptive in environments with high nest predation risk at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The nestling period is followed by a phase of parental provisioning that continues even after flight feather maturation. Field records indicate that sexual maturation, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and reproductive activation, occurs at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching], a remarkably early age for a passerine of this body size at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This precocial reproductive development may be linked to the species' occupation of relatively stable, low-elevation tropical habitats where extended learning periods are less critical.

The maximum recorded body mass for adult females, representing the ultimate wet weight for females, averages 7.14 grams [Wwi = 7.14 grams], while males achieve a slightly higher asymptotic mass of 7.2 grams [Wwi = 7.2 grams], a modest sexual size dimorphism that is common among monogamous acanthizids. This species exhibits a life-history pace that is relatively fast for its family. The maximum lifespan, extrapolated from congeneric data and adjusted for thermal conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], is estimated at approximately 4.9 years [am = approximately 4.9 years]. This longevity is shorter than that recorded for many temperate-zone passerines but aligns with the accelerated life histories typical of tropical island endemics, where reduced seasonality and lower extrinsic mortality risk may favour a slower pace, although here the pattern appears reversed.

Reproductive output in Gerygone flavolateralis is constrained by clutch size and breeding frequency. Females lay between 1 and 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 3 eggs per clutch], and field observations indicate that they typically produce approximately 2 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches each year]. This low annual reproductive output, when considered alongside the incubation temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] and the rapid postnatal development, suggests a strategy that prioritises offspring quality over quantity. The initiation of first reproduction, marking the time since birth at first brood, occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year, despite having reached puberty much earlier at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay likely reflects the need to acquire a territory and establish a stable pair bond in a competitive social environment.

Comparative analyses with other members of the genus reveal notable differences in the timing of key life-history events. For instance, congeneric species from temperate zones exhibit longer fledging periods, whereas the 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching] observed for the Fan-tailed gerygone is among the shortest recorded for any gerygone at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Similarly, the age at birth of 18 days [ab = 18 days] at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] is relatively brief, likely an adaptation to warm, stable nest microclimates. Physiological studies examining the basal metabolic requirements of nestlings under a body temperature of approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] show that growth rates are optimised within this thermal window. The species' small body size, with females reaching an adult body weight of 7.14 grams [Wwi = 7.14 grams] and males 7.2 grams [Wwi = 7.2 grams], places it among the lighter members of its family, a trait that may facilitate the rapid developmental schedule it exhibits.
